terms.definition: An account in Linux that represents a person or process and controls what that entity can access on the system.
terms.example: ec2-user on an Amazon Linux EC2 instance is a user account

terms.definition: A unique numeric identifier assigned to every Linux user. The kernel uses UIDs internally to track permissions.
terms.example: Root always has UID 0; normal users start at UID 1000

terms.definition: The superuser account in Linux with UID 0 and full administrative privileges over the entire system.
terms.example: Running 'sudo -i' gives you a root shell on EC2

terms.definition: A standard user account created by an administrator for a human being. Has limited privileges and UIDs starting at 1000.
terms.example: Creating 'alice' with useradd creates a normal user

terms.definition: An account created automatically for background services and daemons. Not for human login. UIDs typically 1–999.
terms.example: www-data runs the Apache web server process

terms.definition: A collection of Linux user accounts that share a set of permissions, allowing bulk access management.
terms.example: Adding all developers to a 'devs' group so they share access to a project folder

terms.definition: A unique numeric identifier assigned to every Linux group. The kernel uses GIDs to evaluate group-based permissions.
terms.example: The 'devs' group might have GID 1001

terms.definition: The default group automatically created with the same name as the user when a new user account is created.
terms.example: Creating user 'alice' also creates group 'alice' as her primary group

terms.definition: Any additional group a user is added to beyond their primary group, granting shared access to group-owned resources.
terms.example: Adding alice to the 'wheel' group lets her use sudo

terms.definition: The main user database file listing all accounts with their username, UID, GID, home directory, and shell. World-readable.
terms.example: cat /etc/passwd shows all user accounts on the system

terms.definition: The file storing encrypted (hashed) user passwords. Readable only by root for security.
terms.example: sudo cat /etc/shadow reveals hashed passwords

terms.definition: The group database file listing all groups, their GIDs, and member lists.
terms.example: cat /etc/group | grep devs shows devs group members

terms.definition: The configuration file controlling which users and groups can use sudo and which commands they can run.
terms.example: ec2-user is listed in sudoers with NOPASSWD:ALL on Amazon Linux

terms.definition: A command that allows authorised users to run commands with root privileges temporarily without switching to root.
terms.example: sudo yum install httpd installs Apache as root

terms.definition: The command to change file or directory permissions. Accepts symbolic (u+x) or octal (755) notation.
terms.example: chmod 644 file.txt gives owner rw, group and others r only

terms.definition: The command to change the user and/or group ownership of a file or directory. Requires root/sudo.
terms.example: chown alice:devs project/ changes owner to alice and group to devs

terms.definition: The 10-character string shown by ls -l describing file type and three sets of rwx permissions for owner, group, and others.
terms.example: -rwxr-xr-- means regular file, owner rwx, group r-x, others r--

terms.definition: Numeric permission representation where r=4, w=2, x=1. Three digits cover owner, group, and others.
terms.example: chmod 755 sets rwxr-xr-x; 644 sets rw-r--r--

terms.definition: A special permission bit that makes a file execute with its owner's privileges rather than the executing user's privileges.
terms.example: /usr/bin/passwd has SUID so any user can update their own password in /etc/shadow

terms.definition: A special permission bit that on directories causes new files to inherit the directory's group rather than the creator's primary group.
terms.example: A shared project directory with SGID ensures all new files belong to the project group

terms.definition: A special permission bit on directories that restricts file deletion to only the file owner, directory owner, or root.
terms.example: /tmp has the sticky bit — users can create files but not delete each other's

terms.definition: A value subtracted from maximum default permissions (666 for files, 777 for directories) to set the actual permissions of newly created files.
terms.example: umask 022 results in 644 for new files and 755 for new directories

terms.definition: On RHEL/CentOS/Amazon Linux systems, the group whose members are granted sudo privileges by default via /etc/sudoers.
terms.example: sudo usermod -aG wheel alice gives alice sudo access on Amazon Linux

terms.definition: Switch User — allows you to switch to another user account in the current terminal session.
terms.example: su - alice switches to alice's account loading her full environment
